## The idea

This project adds vertical responsibility. Choose a short song, hymn, or
keyboard miniature with melody, bass, and inner harmony. Encode those roles as
three independent structures on one shared timeline. The result should read
like a score model, not a long sequence of play and sleep calls.
It assumes the Roman-numeral engine from
[Lesson 28](../06-chords-and-harmony/28-diatonic-chords-roman-numerals.qmd),
voice-leading checks from
[Lesson 31](../06-chords-and-harmony/31-voice-leading-optimisation-problem.qmd),
and independent timelines from
[Lesson 47](../10-texture-and-arrangement/47-independent-voices.qmd).

Every bar must satisfy the meter in each active voice. Every chord label must be
checked against the notes that sound during its span. A non-chord tone can be
correct, but it needs a rhythmic or melodic explanation rather than a silent
change to the chord symbol.

Start with strict alignment and plain synths. Arrangement choices come after
the score plays from end to end. Otherwise a long release or heavy effect can
hide an overlap that came from the data.

## Run this

The two-bar model stores melody, bass, and harmony separately. Global starts
place them on one timeline. A thread renders each role, and a small check
compares every final end time.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 70

melody = [
  {note: :e4, start: 0.0, duration: 2.0},
  {note: :g4, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0},
  {note: :f4, start: 4.0, duration: 2.0},
  {note: :e4, start: 6.0, duration: 2.0}
]

bass = [
  {note: :c2, start: 0.0, duration: 4.0},
  {note: :f2, start: 4.0, duration: 4.0}
]

harmony = [
  {notes: chord(:c3, :major), start: 0.0, duration: 4.0, symbol: :I},
  {notes: chord(:f3, :major), start: 4.0, duration: 4.0, symbol: :IV}
]

define :play_events do |events, synth_name, amp|
  use_synth synth_name
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note], release: event[:duration] * 0.85, amp: amp
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
end

ends = [
  melody.last[:start] + melody.last[:duration],
  bass.last[:start] + bass.last[:duration],
  harmony.last[:start] + harmony.last[:duration]
]
raise "parts end at different times" unless ends.uniq.length == 1

in_thread { play_events melody, :piano, 0.85 }
in_thread { play_events bass, :fm, 0.5 }

use_synth :hollow
harmony.each do |event|
  play_chord event[:notes], release: event[:duration] * 0.9, amp: 0.35
  sleep event[:duration]
end
```

The melody moves above sustained roots and quiet triads. All parts end after
eight beats, despite using different event counts and rhythms.

## Change one thing

1. Change the final melody duration to 1.5. The alignment assertion fails
   before playback. Restore it and add a half-beat rest event if the source
   actually contains silence.
2. Change the first melody note from E4 to F-sharp4. The event falls outside C
   major while the chord symbol still says I. Listen to the clash, then decide
   whether the note, chord, or analysis is wrong.
3. Move the bass C up an octave. The harmony stays identical, but the inner
   spacing tightens. Compare clarity before changing any amplitude.

## Why it works

The shared timeline is an interface. Each part owns its score data, while starts
and durations use the same units and origin. That permits independent
renderers, bar checks, muting, and transposition. It also prevents one voice's
sleep sequence from becoming the clock for every other voice.

Chord checking is a pitch-class operation. Convert every sounding note with
note % 12 and compare it with the chord's pitch classes at that time. A mismatch
is a review item. Passing tones, suspensions, and anticipations will produce
intentional mismatches, so record their function rather than forcing every note
into the current triad.

Metric integrity belongs at bar level as well as whole-piece level. Equal final
end times can hide one short bar followed by one long bar. Partition events by
measure, account for rests, and assert the expected total before combining
parts.

The structured representation also supports arrangement. Melody, bass, and
inner harmony can receive different synths, registers, pans, and depth without
changing the score. Keep that rendering layer separate until the harmonic and
metric reports are clean.

## Take it further

Complete a sixteen-to-thirty-two-bar melody-and-accompaniment source. Deliver
three separate score structures, one timeline, per-bar metric checks, and a
report comparing chord pitch classes with every sounding note. Annotate each
intentional non-chord tone. The target sound is a balanced three-part rendering
whose melody, bass, or harmony can be muted independently and whose source data
contains no synth or effect choices.
